questions.q: What was the "Syndicate" in the Congress Party of the 1960s, and who led it?
questions.a: The Syndicate was an informal group of powerful regional Congress bosses (K. Kamaraj, S. Nijalingappa, N. Sanjeeva Reddy, Atulya Ghosh, S.K. Patil) who controlled party organization and candidate selection. A wrong answer (e.g., "it was Indira Gandhi's kitchen cabinet" or "a formal constitutional body") reveals confusion between the party's organizational wing and the Prime Minister's inner circle, and misunderstanding of intra-party democracy in the Congress system.

questions.q: Why did Indira Gandhi choose to nationalize 14 major banks in 1969, and how did it serve both economic and political purposes?
questions.a: Economically, it aimed to redirect credit to agriculture and small industry; politically, it forced a showdown with the Syndicate (who opposed it) and Morarji Desai (Finance Minister), allowing her to portray herself as pro-poor and the Syndicate as pro-rich. A wrong answer focusing only on economics misses the deliberate political calculus: the move was timed before the 1969 Presidential election to brand her as a socialist reformer and split the party on ideological lines.

questions.q: In the 1969 Presidential election, Indira Gandhi supported V.V. Giri as an independent candidate against the official Congress nominee N. Sanjeeva Reddy. What constitutional mechanism allowed her to ask Congress MPs for a "conscience vote"?
questions.a: The President is elected by an electoral college (Article 54) via secret ballot; no party whip can legally bind voters in a Presidential election. Her "conscience vote" appeal exploited this constitutional silence to legitimize cross-voting. A wrong answer citing the anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule, added in 1985) shows ignorance of the historical sequence — the law did not exist in 1969.

questions.q: Compare the social base of the "Old Congress" (pre-1969) and the "New Congress" (Indira Gandhi's Congress (R)) after the 1971 election. Which groups did the new Congress mobilize that the old one did not?
questions.a: Old Congress: broad coalition of landed elites, upper castes, business groups, and regional bosses. New Congress: landless laborers, Dalits, Adivasis, minorities, women, unemployed youth — groups previously mediated by local notables. A wrong answer claiming "the base remained the same" ignores the deliberate shift from patronage networks to direct mass appeal via Garibi Hatao.

questions.q: Evaluate the criticism that "Garibi Hatao was only an election gimmick" by citing two policy actions that followed the slogan and one structural limitation that prevented sustained poverty reduction.
questions.a: Policy actions: (1) 1971–72 land ceiling legislation and stricter tenancy laws; (2) expansion of public sector employment and rural works programs. Structural limitation: the Congress (R) lacked a strong village-level organization to implement redistribution; power remained centralized in Delhi, and local elites captured benefits. A purely dismissive or purely defensive answer fails to weigh both evidence and institutional constraints.

questions.q: Draft a 50-word election manifesto promise for a 1971 candidate of Congress (R) that translates "Garibi Hatao" into three concrete, verifiable commitments for a landless Dalit household in Bihar.
questions.a: Example: "1) Your family will receive a bank loan at 4% for a milch cow within 6 months (Bank Nationalization Act). 2) The landlord's surplus land above ceiling will be redistributed to you by March 1972 (Land Reforms Act). 3) Your children get free mid-day meals in the village school (Central scheme)." A vague promise like "we will remove poverty" shows inability to link slogan to specific, time-bound, institutionalized entitlements.
